About Hitech

Manufacturing with
a larger purpose.

Every pipe eventually becomes part of something bigger.

A farm. A city. A water network. An industrial facility. A piece of infrastructure people depend on.

That larger purpose has shaped Hitech since 1999.

Our perspective

We do not look at the pipe
in isolation.

We look at what it needs to do.

  • Where it will operate.
  • What it will carry.
  • How it will connect.
  • What the project expects from it.

Because manufacturing is only one part of the responsibility.

The real responsibility is building confidence in what leaves the factory and becomes part of a working system.

1999

Since 1999

Built over time. Built to keep progressing.

Hitech began its manufacturing journey in 1999.

Over the years, the organisation has continued to widen its manufacturing capability, strengthen its product portfolio and build the systems required to serve increasingly diverse project requirements.

From smaller diameter distribution needs to large diameter infrastructure applications, the journey has been one of continuous capability building.

Not growth for the sake of scale.Growth with greater responsibility.

Leadership

Reliability begins long before installation.

When a pipe becomes part of a water network, agricultural system, industrial application or infrastructure project, it is expected to keep performing.

That expectation places a responsibility on the manufacturer.

For Hitech, progress means more than producing more.

It means strengthening capability, improving systems, investing in technology and becoming more accountable for what the organisation puts into the market.

The scale may change.

The discipline cannot.

OUR VISION

To build Hitech into a globally trusted name in HDPE piping solutions while contributing to stronger agriculture, water management and critical infrastructure.

OUR MISSION

To manufacture dependable HDPE and PE piping products through capable manufacturing, disciplined quality systems and continuous technological progress for customers in India and international markets.

Hitech Assurance Protocol

Reliability is not a feature. It is a system.

A final test can tell you something about a finished product.

It cannot create the quality that should have been built into everything before it.

The Hitech Assurance Protocol looks at reliability as a connected process from requirement understanding to delivery.

Scroll to move through the eight steps.

The eight steps of the Hitech Assurance Protocol

01 / 08

Requirement & Application

  1. 01 · Requirement & Application
    Before manufacturing begins, the requirement needs to be understood. Application. Operating environment. Dimensions. Applicable standards. Project specific expectations. The clearer the requirement, the stronger the foundation for everything that follows.
  2. 02 · Raw Material Integrity
    The performance of the finished product begins with the material going into it. Material requirements are reviewed against the defined product and project specifications before production.
  3. 03 · Process Control
    Consistency does not happen at the end of the line. Manufacturing needs defined process and dimensional checks throughout production so deviations can be identified before they become finished product issues.
  4. 04 · Testing & Inspection
    Testing verifies whether the product meets defined requirements. Relevant quality and performance checks are carried out against applicable product standards, specifications and project requirements.
  5. 05 · Batch Traceability
    A product should not lose its history once it leaves production. Relevant material, production and finished product information is connected through identification and record keeping requirements.
  6. 06 · Documented Quality Systems
    Quality becomes more dependable when the process behind it is documented. Defined processes, inspections and records create greater consistency, accountability and continuity.
  7. 07 · System Integrity
    The pipe is only one part of the system. Fittings. Fabricated assemblies. Connections. Joining. Where relevant, these elements need to be considered together rather than independently.
  8. 08 · Delivery Discipline
    A technically correct product delivered without coordination can still create project problems. Production, quantities, documentation and dispatch need to be aligned with the agreed supply requirement.

Project De-Risking Guide

Fewer assumptions. Better prepared projects.

Many supply problems begin before the purchase order.

A missing detail. An assumed specification. An unclear fitting requirement. A documentation requirement discovered too late.

Use these questions to prepare a clearer piping enquiry.

0/9

0 of 9 answered

Tick each question once it is clear for your project.

  1. 01

    What will the system carry?

    Water?Wastewater?Industrial fluid?Chemical?Gas?Cable or utility infrastructure?

    Start with the application and medium. They influence almost every decision that follows.

  2. 02

    Where will it operate?

    Above ground or underground?Industrial site or open terrain?Marine or floating environment?

    What temperatures and site conditions should be considered? The installation environment matters.

  3. 03

    What does the specification require?

    Identify what is already defined.

    MaterialDiameterWall thickness or dimensional seriesPressure requirementProduct standardColour or markingJoining method

    If a consultant or project specification exists, share it.

  4. 04

    Have the fittings been planned?

    The pipe route rarely remains straight.

    BendsTeesReducersFlangesFabricated assembliesConnections to existing systems

    Bring fitting requirements into the discussion early.

  5. 05

    What documentation will the project need?

    CertificatesTest documentsInspection requirementsDrawingsApprovalsTraceability records

    Clarify these before supply, not after dispatch.

  6. 06

    What are the quantities?

    Share quantities by size and product wherever available.

    This helps create a more useful commercial and production discussion.

  7. 07

    Where does it need to go?

    Project location affects logistics and delivery planning.

    Mention the site, unloading conditions and any sequencing requirements that may influence dispatch.

  8. 08

    When is it needed?

    A required date is useful. A realistic project schedule is better.

    Share expected delivery dates, phases and priorities wherever available.

  9. 09

    What is still unclear?

    Not every enquiry arrives complete. That is normal.

    Identify the areas still under discussion so assumptions do not silently become commitments.

Hitech Insights

A closer look at
what matters.

Piping decisions sit at the intersection of engineering, manufacturing, procurement and project execution.

Hitech Insights explores the questions behind those decisions.

01

A pipe quotation should tell you more than the price.

  • What exactly is being supplied?
  • Which specification applies?
  • What fittings are included?
  • Which documents are expected?
  • Where will it be delivered?

A clearer quotation begins with a clearer enquiry.

02

Why application should come before product recommendation.

The same material can behave differently across different service conditions.

Understanding the medium, environment, operating requirements and project specification should come before deciding what the product needs to be.

03

The connections deserve as much attention as the straight runs.

A piping network changes direction. It branches. It reduces. It connects to equipment and existing systems.

Planning fittings and fabricated assemblies early can prevent later project complications.

04

Lowest purchase price and lowest project cost are not always the same thing.

Material choice, fittings, handling, installation, maintenance and replacement requirements all influence the economics of a piping system.

The purchase price is one part of a much larger lifecycle decision.

Better questions lead
to better decisions.
